claims.claim: Following US guidelines for 5 conditions in a hypothetical 79-year-old woman gives 12 medicines and a complicated non-drug regimen; most guidelines did not address older people with multiple conditions.
claims.supporting_passage: Most CPGs did not modify or discuss the applicability of their recommendations for older patients with multiple comorbidities. ... If the relevant CPGs were followed, the hypothetical patient would be prescribed 12 medications (costing her 406 dollars per month) and a complicated nonpharmacological regimen. Adverse interactions between drugs and diseases could result.
claims.pico_timeframe: Hypothetical 79-year-old woman with COPD, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, hypertension, osteoarthritis; US/international guidelines circa 2005
claims.safe_wording: A 2005 US analysis added up the guidelines for five common conditions for an imagined 79-year-old woman: she would be prescribed 12 medicines plus a complicated non-drug regimen.
claims.qualifications: Hypothetical patient; US guidelines from 2005; not NICE. Daily dose count not verified (full text not opened) so do not state doses.

numbers.meaning: medications prescribed to one hypothetical patient

claims.claim: Drugs recommended in NICE type 2 diabetes guideline had 133 potentially serious interactions with drugs recommended in guidelines for 11 other conditions; few highlighted.
claims.supporting_passage: 133 drug-drug interactions for drugs recommended in the type 2 diabetes guideline, 89 for depression, and 111 for heart failure. Few of these drug-disease or drug-drug interactions were highlighted in the guidelines for the three index conditions.
claims.pico_timeframe: NICE guidelines for T2DM, depression, heart failure vs drugs recommended for 11 other common conditions
claims.safe_wording: A UK review found 133 potentially serious interactions between drugs recommended in the NICE type 2 diabetes guideline and drugs recommended in NICE guidelines for 11 other common conditions; few were flagged in the guideline.
claims.qualifications: Potential interactions between recommendations, not observed harm in patients.

numbers.meaning: potentially serious drug-drug interactions, T2DM guideline

claims.claim: Following five NICE guidelines for hypothetical patients gives considerable treatment burden and complex follow-up; guidelines give no guidance on prioritising.
claims.supporting_passage: Explicitly following guideline recommendations for our two hypothetical patients would lead to a considerable treatment burden, even when recommendations were followed for mild to moderate conditions. In addition, the follow-up and self-care regime was complex ... current guideline recommendations rapidly cumulate to drive polypharmacy, without providing guidance on how best to prioritise recommendations
claims.pico_timeframe: Five NICE guidelines (2007+), two hypothetical patients
claims.safe_wording: Applying five NICE guidelines to two imagined patients produced a heavy treatment burden and a complex follow-up and self-care routine, with no guidance on which recommendations to put first.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NICE NG56 (multimorbidity) not opened; do not cite it.

claims.claim: No trial tested the combined plan; it should be reviewed as a whole against the person's priorities.
claims.safe_wording: Frame as judgement: 'No single guideline weighed the combined plan, so we should review it as one plan against what matters most to the person.'
claims.qualifications: Ethical/clinical judgement, not a finding. Do not cite NICE NG56 (not opened).

claims.claim: Of 434 JAGS research articles 2008-09, at least 29% explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment; 6% gave justification; 14% discussed as limitation.
claims.supporting_passage: Of 434 articles examined, 16% used recruitment methods likely to reduce participation by persons with cognitive impairment. At least 29% of studies (n = 127) employed explicit exclusion criteria. ... Few (6%) provided any justification for exclusion criteria used, only 43% gave any reason for exclusion, and only 14% discussed exclusion as a possible limitation.
claims.pico_timeframe: All 434 original research articles, J Am Geriatr Soc, 2008-2009
claims.safe_wording: In two years of a leading geriatrics journal, at least 127 of 434 studies (29%) explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment, and very few gave any justification for doing so.
claims.qualifications: The abstract does not state whether 6% and 14% are of 434 or of the 127; avoid '6 in 100' unless full text confirms. One US journal, 2008-09.

claims.claim: Few recently completed UK trials in conditions linked with cognitive impairment included adults who lacked capacity.
claims.supporting_passage: We identified 81 trials in the conditions or populations searched for which were completed between 2015 and 2018, of which 15 trials (18%) allowed for the inclusion of adults who lacked capacity
claims.location: Full text, Main text (abstract says 80 retrieved trials)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK ISRCTN-registered trials completed 2015-2018 in conditions such as dementia, critical care
claims.safe_wording: Of about 80 UK trials completed 2015-2018 in conditions where impaired capacity is common, only 15 allowed adults who lacked capacity to take part.
claims.qualifications: Say 'about 80' or '15 of 81' given abstract/full-text discrepancy; search not comprehensive.

claims.claim: UK law (England and Wales) allows adults lacking capacity to take part in research with safeguards via consultees/legal representatives.
claims.supporting_passage: In England and Wales, the legal frameworks govern the inclusion of adults who lack capacity in clinical trials of medicinal products under the Medicines for Human Use (Clinical Trials) Regulations 2004 [], with other types of research governed by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 []. Under this legal framework, someone who knows the person who lacks capacity is approached by the researcher to act as their legal representative or consultee.
claims.safe_wording: In England and Wales, the law already allows adults who lack capacity to take part in research: drug trials under the Clinical Trials Regulations 2004 with a legal representative's consent, and other research under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 with a consultee's advice.
claims.qualifications: England and Wales only. Scottish law (Adults with Incapacity Act s51) not verified: do not state details; say only that Scotland has its own legislation, or omit.

claims.claim: Adults with impaired capacity are frequently excluded partly because researchers are unfamiliar with legal frameworks; INCLUDE framework exists to help.
claims.supporting_passage: adults with impaired capacity to consent are frequently excluded from trials - partly because researchers are unfamiliar with the legal and ethical frameworks and lack the necessary methodological expertise. ... The framework has two parts: a set of four key questions to help researchers identify who should be included in their trial, and a series of worksheets
claims.safe_wording: A UK framework (INCLUDE Impaired Capacity to Consent) gives trial teams four key questions and worksheets to design trials that include people who lack capacity.
claims.qualifications: Its effect on inclusion is not yet evaluated.

claims.claim: In Scotland, onset of multimorbidity occurred 10-15 years earlier in the most deprived than most affluent areas.
claims.supporting_passage: Onset of multimorbidity occurred 10-15 years earlier in people living in the most deprived areas compared with the most affluent
claims.pico_timeframe: 1,751,841 people, 314 Scottish practices, March 2007; multimorbidity = 2+ of 40 conditions
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 1.75 million people in Scotland, having two or more long-term conditions became common 10 to 15 years earlier in the most deprived areas than in the most affluent.
claims.qualifications: Population-level, cross-sectional 2007 data; not a statement about individuals. Chart values not verified (full text not opened): no chart figures.

numbers.meaning: population difference in age of onset

claims.claim: More people with multimorbidity were under 65 than over 65.
claims.supporting_passage: the absolute number of people with multimorbidity was higher in those younger than 65 years (210,500 vs 194,996)
claims.safe_wording: In that Scottish study, more people with two or more long-term conditions were under 65 (210,500) than 65 or over (194,996), although the proportion was highest in older people.

claims.claim: Healthy life expectancy gap by deprivation.
Standard survival analysis overestimated 5- and 10-year risk of second hip fracture vs competing-risk method.
claims.supporting_passage: Using traditional survival analysis ... the incidence of second hip fracture at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years was 3%, 7%, 11%, and 21%, respectively. A competing risk approach resulted in a lower estimate of incidence: 3%, 6%, 8%, and 12%, respectively. ... During follow-up, a much greater proportion of subjects died without experiencing a second hip fracture (73%)
claims.pico_timeframe: 481 Framingham members with first hip fracture 1948-2003
claims.safe_wording: In 481 people after a first hip fracture, the usual method put the 10-year risk of a second hip fracture at 21 in 100; allowing for deaths from other causes gave 12 in 100. 73% died without a second fracture.
claims.qualifications: One cohort; the gap grows with follow-up length and mortality. Do not imply FRAX shares the flaw.

claims.claim: A trial with 80% power for the overall effect has only 29% power to detect an interaction of the same size; ~fourfold sample needed; subgroup-specific tests often give spurious results.
claims.supporting_passage: a trial with 80% power for the overall effect had only 29% power to detect an interaction effect of the same magnitude. For interactions of this size to be detected with the same power as the overall effect, sample sizes should be inflated fourfold ... A significant effect in one subgroup only was observed in 7% to 64% of simulations
claims.safe_wording: In simulations, a trial designed with 80% power for its main result had only 29% power to detect a subgroup difference of the same size; about four times the participants would be needed. Apparent effects in one subgroup only were also common by chance.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No real trial's oldest subgroup numbers verified.

candidates.reason: Boyd, Dumbreck and Hughes abstracts support the core with qualifications (hypothetical patients; potential not observed interactions). Combined-plan review is judgement.
Taylor and Shepherd support; 6% denominator unclear; Scottish law and Clinical Trials Regulations detail not verified from legislation.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep to England and Wales legal route (sourced from Shepherd 2019), use '127 of 434 excluded; very few justified it', and '15 of about 80 UK trials'; label inclusion-by-default as ethical judgement; omit Scottish s51 detail.

candidates.reason: Barnett supports core; healthy life expectancy claim unsourced; no concrete age-gated example verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Build on Barnett alone (10-15 years earlier onset; population level); drop healthy life expectancy; keep need-based entry as judgement; any named age-gated example needs its own source.

candidates.reason: Absolute pair 21% vs 12% confirmed in full text (reserve).
Brookes figures confirmed; no real-trial oldest subgroup example verified (reserve).
candidates.revised_angle: Teach with Brookes numbers and a two-way caution; use no named trial example unless separately verified.
